entry.title: SQL Joins & Window Functions
entry.summary:
Introduction
SQL joins are used to combine data from multiple tables based on a related column. Window functions , on the other hand perform calculations across a set of table rows related to the current row, enabling row-wise aggregations without collapsing the data There are four main types of SQL joins Inner join - returns only the records that have matching values in both tables.
Which customers have placed orders? Assume we have two tables: Customers Orders
To answer this question, you'd write this query SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, o.order_id FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

entry.title: Pagination & Filtering: Managing Large Datasets Efficiently with FastAPI
entry.summary:
Why Pagination Matters
Imagine an API returning 10,000 items at once. Pagination solves this by slicing data into @app.get("/items") def get_items( page: int = Query(default=1, ge=1), limit: int = Query(default=5, ge=1, le=20), category: Optional[str] = None, min_price: Optional[float] = None, max_price: Optional[float] = None ):
offset = (page - 1) * limit items = query.offset(offset).limit(limit).all()
page=1, limit=5 → items 1-5 page=2, limit=5 → items 6-10 page=3, limit=5 → items 11-15 The offset tells the database where to start, The same endpoint handles filtering: ?category=electronics → only electronics ?min_price=100&max_price=500 → price range filter ?category=electronics&page=2&limit=5 → combined! { "metadata": { "total": 12, "page": 2, "limit": 5, "total_pages": 3 }, "data": [...] }
Always return metadata with paginated responses,

entry.title: Escaping the Sea of Sameness: "Core" Path vs "Creative" Path
entry.summary:
In my last post, I mentioned a "pivot." But tody we have another story of another pivot 🫣 When I started this journey, I did exactly what you are supposed to do. I pulled up the roadmaps. I looked at the "Frontend Developer" path (HTML, CSS, JS) and I started walking.But while my brain was trying to memorize syntax, my heart was cheating on the curriculum. The "Right" Way vs. The "Real" Way
Every time I was supposed to be studying any logical structure, I found myself drifting toward Animated Websites. I was obsessing over visuals, over the "feel" of a site, over 3D objects that you could spin and touch. But here is the paradox every creative person faces: To be a great designer, I realized I had to become a coder. Also, we need to talk about the state of the modern web. I found myself getting nostalgic for the internet of the early 2000s. Remember Flash? Remember when websites had textures, sounds, and weird navigation? It was chaotic, sure, but it was rich. It had personality. It felt human. Modern minimalism has stripped the soul out of the web in the name of efficiency. And with the rise of AI—which can generate "clean" code and standard layouts in seconds—the "Standard" developer is becoming a commodity. This frustration grew until I couldn't ignore it. I realized I don't want to be a "Full Stack Developer." I don't want to fit into that box. The Core Developer builds the engine. The Creative Developer paints the chassis and makes sure the car looks like it's breaking the sound barrier. I am pivoting to this path not because it’s easy—Three.js, WebGL, and Shaders are hard—but because it is the only way to save my creative identity. I’m here to make the web weird again. I’m here to make it fun. If you’re tired too of building the same dashboard over and over again, maybe you should join me.
